steps.text: Ensure your stethoscope has been cleaned according to local infection prevention and control guidance.
Discuss the procedure with the patient and gain informed consent.
Keep the patient warm and the area free from drafts.
Screen the bed to maintain privacy and dignity.
Decontaminate your hands.
Position the patient comfortably so you can access their chest (ideally sitting in a chair or on the side of the bed; some tolerate only 45°).
Remove or rearrange clothing as needed to see the chest.
Warm the stethoscope between your hands if it feels cold.
Put the ear tips in pointing slightly forward, towards the nose.
Hold the chest piece between the index and middle finger of your dominant hand and place it flat on the chest with gentle pressure.
Anterior chest: use a 'stepladder' approach from the 1st to the 7th intercostal space, comparing side to side; listen for a full inspiration and expiration at each point.
Posterior chest: stepladder approach from the 1st to the 7th intercostal space, avoiding the scapula.
Right lateral chest: ask the patient to move their right arm aside; listen upper, then middle, then lower lobe.
Repeat on the left side (upper and lower lobes).
Replace the patient's clothing and make them comfortable.
Explain your findings and check whether the patient has any questions.
Decontaminate your stethoscope.
Decontaminate your hands.
Record findings: location of auscultation, quality, and where any abnormal sounds were heard.
Perform hand hygiene and gather stethoscope and watch.
Introduce yourself, explain the assessment and obtain consent.
Position the patient upright where possible and expose only as required.
Assess general appearance, colour and work of breathing.
Count respiratory rate for one full minute; assess rhythm, depth and effort.
Inspect anterior and posterior thorax for shape, symmetry, scars and bruising.
Palpate posterior chest for temperature, tenderness, masses and expansion.
Percuss posterior chest systematically.
Auscultate posterior chest systematically and assess vocal resonance where appropriate.
Palpate anterior chest, including tracheal position and expansion.
Percuss and auscultate anterior chest and trachea systematically.
Identify and describe normal and adventitious breath sounds.
Reposition the patient, ensure comfort, clean equipment and perform hand hygiene.
Document findings accurately and escalate significant changes.
Position the patient upright.
Ask the patient to breathe through their mouth.
Listen to breath sounds with your stethoscope at each auscultation point, anterior and posterior chest.
Compare each side with the other.
Listen for quality, intensity and adventitious sounds.
If you hear stridor (a loud strangulating sound on inspiration, clearest over the trachea), get an immediate review by a senior doctor.

notes.text: 93225 summary: ideally position the patient upright and have them breathe through their mouth; listen comparing each side with the other; listen for quality, intensity and adventitious (unexpected) sounds.

Stethoscope: bell for high-pitched sounds at the lung apex above the clavicle; diaphragm for low-pitched sounds over the rest of the chest. Lung sounds cannot be heard through bone, so avoid the scapula.

Normal breath sounds: tracheal (very loud, high pitch, over the trachea); bronchial (loud, over the manubrium); bronchovesicular (medium, 1st-2nd intercostal spaces beside the sternum and between the scapulae); vesicular (soft, low pitch, inspiration longer than expiration, most of the lung field).

Crackles: from small airways, mostly on inspiration. Coarse crackles may indicate pneumonia, fine crackles may suggest pulmonary oedema; seen in pneumonia, pulmonary fibrosis, COPD, infection and heart failure. Wheeze: often expiratory, musical; high-pitched in asthma. Inspiratory wheeze (stridor) usually means upper airway obstruction. Absent breath sounds: e.g. pneumothorax, pleural effusion, consolidation.
Stridor needs an immediate review by a senior doctor, and a silent chest may mean total peripheral airway obstruction (FNP2B tutorial).
